name: Plasma pen (fibroblasting)

card.summary: A handheld device that arcs ionised gas onto the skin, marketed for eyelid and skin tightening; no controlled trials for cosmetic tightening were found.
card.aka: Plasma pen, fibroblast plasma, plasma lift, non-surgical blepharoplasty, plasma fibroblasting
card.price: $40-60 for devices; $400-1,900 per clinic treatment (forum figures)
card.note: Cosmetic skin-tightening claims lack published trials; online forum posts describe home use on the eyelids.

quick.overview:
A plasma pen is a small handheld device that produces a tiny electrical arc of ionised gas between its tip and the skin. In cosmetic use it is marketed as 'fibroblasting' for tightening sagging or hooded eyelids, smoothing lines and removing small skin lesions without cutting.
It appears in looksmaxxing forums as a cheap alternative to eyelid surgery, with posts pointing to inexpensive consumer devices and much costlier clinic treatments. No controlled trials of the cosmetic tightening claim have been published.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the arc heats tiny points of the skin surface, producing small controlled injuries that prompt a repair response by fibroblasts and tighten the area; this explanation was not found in published studies. Scientific literature on 'plasma pens' mainly covers cold atmospheric plasma used for disinfection and wound research, which is a different application from cosmetic burning.
quick.risks: Because the cosmetic method works by creating small burns and no cosmetic safety trial has been published, complication rates are unknown. A 2025 case report describes plasma pen ablation used clinically for extensive periocular xanthogranuloma.

lead: A plasma pen is a handheld device that generates a small electrical arc of ionised gas, or plasma, between its tip and the skin. Marketed in cosmetics as fibroblasting, fibroblast plasma or a plasma lift, it is used to tighten loose skin, particularly on the upper eyelids (sometimes sold as non-surgical blepharoplasty), to smooth lines, and to remove small blemishes such as moles and skin tags.[3][8]

The device is applied in rows of tiny dots. Practitioners and the authors of case reports describe the arcs as delivering controlled thermal energy that removes damaged surface skin and is believed to stimulate fibroblasts and new collagen in the upper dermis, although the exact mechanism is described as debated.[8] People use it to look less tired and heavy-lidded and to firm skin around the eyes, nose folds, forehead and neck without surgery.[3]

Plasma itself is described as the fourth state of matter, and cold atmospheric plasma has been studied for disinfection, wound care, dermatology and dentistry.[1][2][17] Research specific to cosmetic plasma pens consists mainly of social-media analyses and case reports rather than controlled trials of skin tightening.[10][11][12] A separate, older body of clinical work covers 'plasma skin regeneration' devices used in clinics for facial rejuvenation, and the pen is often described as a cheaper, hand-held relative of that technology.[8][17]

In looksmaxxing forums the pen is presented as a low-cost route to improved eyelids and skin, with users quoting device prices and comparing them with clinic fees.[3] It sits alongside lasers, radiofrequency, microneedling and eyelid surgery in discussions of the eye area.

paras: The main appearance goal is the upper eyelid: loose or hooded skin that makes the eyes look smaller or tired. Marketers call the pen a 'non-surgical blepharoplasty', and the clinical literature describes use mainly for mild upper-eyelid skin excess and for fine lines and wrinkles around the lower lids.[8] Other advertised sites are the nasal folds, forehead and neck, and the pen is also sold for removing small lesions.[3][11]

In looksmaxxing discussion the eye area is treated as a high-impact feature, and the pen is pitched as a way to improve it for far less than surgery.[3] Upper-eyelid blepharoplasty, by comparison, is an outpatient operation of about one to three hours in which an incision in the natural crease is used to remove excess skin, muscle and sometimes fat; bruising and swelling generally resolve over several weeks.[16]

A plasma fibroblast device is described as an ultra-high-frequency generator that turns atmospheric nitrogen into plasma and delivers controlled thermal energy to the skin through a handpiece, in a grid of dots.[8] The heat is believed to remove old, photodamaged epidermal cells and to stimulate fibroblasts and collagen growth in the upper dermis.[8] The authors of a 2020 case report state that the exact mechanism is debated.[8]

Proponents describe the effect as superficial tissue sublimation followed by skin contraction and repair, with results said to appear as the small crusts heal.[3] The treatment intentionally creates small thermal injuries.[8][10]

The idea of using plasma energy on skin predates the pen boom. Clinical journals from 2007 and 2008 describe studies of 'plasma skin regeneration' devices (the Portrait system) for full-face rejuvenation, including work by Bogle, Arndt and Dover in Archives of Dermatology and a pilot study by Kilmer and colleagues in Lasers in Medical Science.[17] The case report literature cites earlier descriptions of plasma delivering thermal energy to skin from 2008 and 2014.[8]

subs.h: From clinic devices to handheld pens
paras: A Chinese patent record from 2008 describes a minisize plasma pen for removing skin speckle.[14] Handheld units later appeared on the high street and online; a UK case report describes plasma fibroblast treatment as a relatively new, growing and increasingly available minimally invasive aesthetic procedure.[8]

Researchers who study social media describe how the pen spread through short-video platforms: a 2022 analysis of TikTok posts on pen and fibroblast hashtags, and a 2022 analysis of Instagram 'mole removal' hashtags, both treat it as an example of non-regulated cosmetic devices travelling through online influence.[10][11]

Treatments are offered by salons and clinics and, through consumer devices, at home. Practitioners and marketers describe applying the arc in rows or grids of tiny dots to the target skin, with a numbing cream commonly used beforehand and small crusts forming and shedding afterwards.[3][8] This article does not provide technique details.

The Instagram analysis found that among non-physician providers of mole removal, the plasma pen was the most-used method, at 97.9 percent in Turkey and 75 percent worldwide; physicians made up a larger share of providers in countries such as India and the United States.[11] The TikTok study started from 200 posts and analysed 122 after removing duplicates, deleted posts and non-English posts.[10]

The cosmetic technique intentionally creates small thermal injuries. Temporary hyperpigmentation is often reported, particularly at higher energy settings, according to the authors of one case report.[8] Reviews of social-media use list dyspigmentation, scarring and burns as potential adverse effects, and note that many commercially sold pens are not FDA-regulated.[10]

Published case reports describe individual harms. In a 2020 BMC Ophthalmology report, a 60-year-old woman had eyelid treatment at a salon during which numbing cream seeped into both eyes. About four hours later she had painful, red, light-sensitive eyes with alkaline chemical injury and roughly 80 percent corneal epithelial loss in each eye, plus dot-like burn marks on the skin. Her vision returned to 6/6 in both eyes and the surface was normal by day 25 apart from mild dry eye, and she was advised she remained at risk of recurrent corneal erosion.[8] The authors present it as the first reported bilateral chemical eye injury from this treatment and give no incidence figures.[8]

A 2024 Cureus case report describes a second-degree burn over the breast after an attempted tightening with a PlasmaPen, presented by the authors as an example of risks of procedures popularised on social media.[12] Reference sources also note that arcing becomes possible at higher power settings with close electrode spacing.[2]

The word plasma appears in medicine in other senses. Cold atmospheric plasma devices, including a veterinary pen, have been tested against bacteria for keratitis,[4] and wound-treatment uses of cold plasma are described in reference works.[2] A 2019 review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity and a 2010 review in the Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft survey cold atmospheric plasma in dermatology.[17] Studies of tissue-tolerable plasma on pig eyes examined tolerance and antiseptic efficacy for wound applications rather than for cosmetic use.[5] A 2025 case report describes plasma pen ablation used clinically for extensive periocular xanthogranuloma.[6]

Name confusion is common: a 2026 study of 'Plasma IQ', a microcurrent radiofrequency device that does not generate plasma gas, treated 30 people with facial laxity and reported a 22.51 percent gain in skin elasticity at 90 days and about 2 mm greater eyelid margin-to-fold distance, but it is a different technology from the arc pen.[18]

No studies found of cosmetic skin tightening with plasma pens in controlled trials. Published human literature consists of case reports and social-media analyses: a 2020 case report of chemical eye injury during salon eyelid treatment,[8] a 2024 report of a burn after attempted breast tightening,[12] a 2025 case report of plasma pen ablation for periocular xanthogranuloma,[6] and content analyses of TikTok and Instagram posts.[10][11]

Clinic-grade plasma skin regeneration devices have been examined in pilot studies of full-face rejuvenation, which are different devices from consumer pens.[17] Related research on cold plasma covers disinfection of wounds and the eye in animals and laboratory models, including argon plasma against canine keratitis pathogens and on canine corneas ex vivo (20 eyes, 2- and 5-minute treatments), as well as a plasma-activated liquid study on cancer cell lines.[4][7][13] These test biomedical plasma devices, not cosmetic tightening.

A looksmax.org thread describes the plasma pen as a way to rejuvenate sagging, wrinkled and dull skin, saying devices cost roughly $40-60 while clinic treatment ranges from $400 to $1,900, and names eyelids, nasal folds, forehead and neck as the most common treated areas.[3] A reply says the user would try it when undereyes decline.[3]

The thread frames the pen as a way to ascend by improving the eye area, suggesting treating the whole eye region. Online comment is part of a wider social-media trend that dermatology researchers have examined for the spread of non-regulated cosmetic devices.[3][10]

Looksmaxxing as a subculture is described by Wikipedia as arising from 2010s online forums and spreading to TikTok in the early 2020s, the same period in which short-video platforms spread the pen.[19] Upper-eyelid surgery is the standard clinical comparison the community uses, which is why forum posters frame the pen's low price against clinic fees and surgery.[3][16]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org posts present the plasma pen as an affordable alternative for eyelid and skin rejuvenation.[3]

claims.claim: A plasma pen can tighten eyelids and give 'baby-skin'.
claims.believers: A forum thread says plasma pens rejuvenate sagging, wrinkled and dull skin, with eyelids, nasal folds, forehead and neck as the best areas, and suggests treating the whole eye area.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies were found that test cosmetic skin tightening with plasma pens; published plasma research concerns disinfection and wound-related effects.[4][5]

claims.claim: Home plasma pens at $40-60 are an economical substitute for $400-1,900 clinic treatments.
claims.believers: The same thread contrasts consumer device prices with clinic fees and says results justify the cost.[3]
claims.experts: No head-to-head comparison of consumer and clinic devices has been published. The TikTok analysis notes that many commercially sold pens are not FDA-regulated.[10]

claims.claim: Plasma pens can remove moles and skin lesions at home or in salons
claims.believers: Social-media providers market the pen for mole removal; among non-physician Instagram providers it was the most used method.[11]
claims.experts: The authors of the Instagram analysis examined who offers these treatments and by what method; the TikTok study lists scarring and dyspigmentation as potential harms.[10][11]

claims.claim: Treating the whole eye area with a plasma pen is the way to improve it.
claims.believers: The forum thread suggests treating the whole eye region and frames the pen as an ascension tool for the eye area.[3]
claims.experts: The clinical literature describes use mainly for mild upper-eyelid skin excess and fine lines, and its authors call the mechanism debated.[8]

claims.claim: Salon plasma treatments are a safe, minor procedure.
claims.believers: Marketing describes the treatment as non-surgical, with dot-like crusts that heal.[3][8]
claims.experts: A BMC Ophthalmology case report documented bilateral chemical eye injury during salon eyelid treatment, and social-media studies list dyspigmentation, scarring and burns as potential adverse effects.[8][10]

claims.claim: Plasma pens are the same as clinical plasma skin devices.
claims.believers: Sellers describe plasma pens as delivering the same plasma-based tightening seen in clinics.[3]
claims.experts: Clinical studies from 2007-2008 examined a specific plasma skin regeneration system; no published trial has compared it with consumer pens, and the TikTok analysis notes that many pens are not FDA-regulated.[10][17]

claims.claim: The plasma pen can replace eyelid surgery.
claims.believers: Forum users present it as a cheaper alternative for hooded or sagging eyelids.[3]
claims.experts: Eyelid surgery excises excess skin, muscle and sometimes fat; the pen's literature consists of case reports and no controlled trial of tightening has been published.[16][12]

angle.text: Users and practitioners apply a plasma pen to the eyelids, nasal folds, forehead and neck, aiming for tighter, smoother skin and a less hooded eye area without a scalpel. Forum posts quote consumer devices at tens of dollars and clinic sessions at hundreds.
